questions.wording: Were data for this outcome available for all, or nearly all, participants randomized?
questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the extent of missing outcome data remains unknown after bounded retrieval. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

questions.wording: If N/PN/NI to 3.1: Is there evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data?
questions.official_guidance: Evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data may come from analysis methods that correct for bias, or sensitivity analyses showing that results are little changed under a range of plausible assumptions about the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value. However, imputing the outcome variable, either through methods such as ‘last-observation-carried-forward’ or via multiple imputation based only on intervention group, should not be assumed to correct for bias due to missing outcome data.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.2
questions.bias_construct: Whether there is evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data.
questions.decision_rule: Evidence may come from methods correcting for bias or sensitivity analyses showing little change under plausible assumptions about missingness and true outcome. The assumptions must match the documented missingness mechanism and the approved Result. A comparison that changes group attribution, such as ITT versus as-treated, does not test unobserved outcome values unless the source explicitly establishes that relationship. Last-observation-carried-forward or multiple imputation based only on intervention group should not be assumed to correct bias.
evidence_needed: A bias-correcting analysis or sensitivity analysis with plausible missingness assumptions and its result, including the missingness mechanism it addresses.
If the source only changes intervention-group attribution or analysis membership, record that distinction; do not describe it as a test of unobserved outcome values without source support.
questions.no_information_rule: No_information is not an allowed response to this question in the parallel-assignment pack. No does not assert that bias occurred: retain source coverage limits and unknown missingness mechanisms. Ground the scoped negative answer in inspected Evidence or a valid scoped no-hit receipt; an unsupported limitation alone is insufficient.

answer_anchors.text: A bias-correcting or informative sensitivity analysis indicates the result was not biased.

considerations: Imputation alone is not evidence that missing outcome data did not bias the result.

questions.wording: If N/PN to 3.2: Could missingness in the outcome depend on its true value?
questions.official_guidance: If loss to follow up, or withdrawal from the study, could be related to participants’ health status, then it is possible that missingness in the outcome was influenced by its true value. However, if all missing outcome data occurred for documented reasons that are unrelated to the outcome then the risk of bias due to missing outcome data will be low.

questions.bias_construct: Whether missingness in the outcome could depend on its true value.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when loss to follow-up or withdrawal could relate to health status or outcome. Answer no or probably no when all missingness had documented reasons unrelated to outcome, such as a failed measuring device or interruption to routine data collection.
evidence_needed: Reasons for missingness and their relationship to participants' health status or true outcome, including censoring and treatment switching in time-to-event analyses.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when the reasons for missingness do not permit assessment of dependence on the true value.

answer_anchors.text: Missingness could depend on the true outcome value.
Documented missingness reasons are unrelated to the outcome.

considerations: For time-to-event outcomes, inspect censoring reasons and timing to identify missing follow-up. A common administrative cutoff does not by itself establish outcome-dependent missingness.

Separate observed outcome data, analysed membership, follow-up availability, and the missingness mechanism. Treatment discontinuation is not loss to follow-up when outcome ascertainment continues; stopping treatment or an analysis label alone does not establish whether the outcome was observed. Last-known-alive censoring is not by itself evidence that observation stopped. This question asks whether the missingness mechanism could depend on the true value; it is not a question about analysis membership.

Withdrawal or censoring after worsening health or symptoms can support possible dependence on the outcome value when the source links the reason to that participant's outcome; stopping treatment without that follow-up loss does not.
invalid_shortcuts: a reason for withdrawal without its relation to outcome

questions.wording: If Y/PY/NI to 3.3: Is it likely that missingness in the outcome depended on its true value?
questions.official_guidance: This question distinguishes between situations in which (i) missingness could depend on its true value and (ii) it is likely that missingness depended on its true value. Five reasons for answering ‘Yes’ are differences between intervention groups in the proportions of missing outcome data; reported reasons that provide evidence that missingness depends on its true value; reasons that differ between intervention groups; trial circumstances; and censoring when participants stop or change their assigned intervention.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance pp. 45-46, Box 8, signalling question 3.4
questions.bias_construct: Whether missingness that could depend on true value likely depended on it.
questions.decision_rule: Consider differences in missingness or censoring rates, reasons that depend on true value, reasons differing between groups, trial circumstances, and censoring after stopping or changing intervention. Answer no when analysis accounted for participant characteristics likely to explain the relationship.
evidence_needed: Group-specific missingness or censoring, reasons for missingness, trial circumstances, and any analysis accounting for relevant participant characteristics.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when likelihood of dependence on true value cannot be judged from the available evidence.

answer_anchors.text: Missingness likely depended on the true outcome value.
The analysis accounted for characteristics explaining the relationship, or dependence was not likely.

considerations: Possible dependence in 3.3 does not establish likely dependence in 3.4. Judge likelihood from missingness reasons and trial circumstances; absent contrary evidence alone does not establish likelihood.

Keep the stages distinct: observed outcome data and follow-up availability describe what was obtained; 3.3 asks whether missingness could depend on the true value; 3.4 asks whether that dependence was likely. Do not promote possible dependence to likely dependence without supporting evidence.

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.

sections.excerpt: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.2
sections.excerpt: Evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data may come from analysis methods that correct for bias, or sensitivity analyses showing that results are little changed under a range of plausible assumptions about the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value. However, imputing the outcome variable, either through methods such as ‘last-observation-carried-forward’ or via multiple imputation based only on intervention group, should not be assumed to correct for bias due to missing outcome data.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.3
sections.excerpt: If loss to follow up, or withdrawal from the study, could be related to participants’ health status, then it is possible that missingness in the outcome was influenced by its true value. However, if all missing outcome data occurred for documented reasons that are unrelated to the outcome then the risk of bias due to missing outcome data will be low.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance pp. 45-46, Box 8, signalling question 3.4
sections.excerpt: This question distinguishes between situations in which (i) missingness could depend on its true value and (ii) it is likely that missingness depended on its true value. Five reasons for answering ‘Yes’ are differences between intervention groups in the proportions of missing outcome data; reported reasons that provide evidence that missingness depends on its true value; reasons that differ between intervention groups; trial circumstances; and censoring when participants stop or change their assigned intervention.

19|BACKGROUND
20|Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors reduce the risk of hospitaliza-
21|tion for heart failure and cardiovascular death among patients with chronic heart
22|failure and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40% or less. Whether SGLT2 in-
23|hibitors are effective in patients with a higher left ventricular ejection fraction
24|remains less certain.
25|METHODS
26|We randomly assigned 6263 patients with heart failure and a left ventricular ejec-
27|tion fraction of more than 40% to receive dapagliflozin (at a dose of 10 mg once
28|daily) or matching placebo, in addition to usual therapy. The primary outcome was
29|a composite of worsening heart failure (which was defined as either an unplanned
30|hospitalization for heart failure or an urgent visit for heart failure) or cardiovas-
31|cular death, as assessed in a time-to-event analysis.
32|RESULTS
33|Over a median of 2.3 years, the primary outcome occurred in 512 of 3131 patients
34|(16.4%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 610 of 3132 patients (19.5%) in the pla-
35|cebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.73 to 0.92; P<0.001).
36|Worsening heart failure occurred in 368 patients (11.8%) in the dapagliflozin
37|group and in 455 patients (14.5%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95%
38|CI, 0.69 to 0.91); cardiovascular death occurred in 231 patients (7.4%) and 261
39|patients (8.3%), respectively (hazard ratio, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.74 to 1.05). Total events
40|and symptom burden were lower in the dapagliflozin group than in the placebo
41|group. Results were similar among patients with a left ventricular ejection fraction
42|of 60% or more and those with a left ventricular ejection fraction of less than 60%,
43|and results were similar in prespecified subgroups, including patients with or
44|without diabetes. The incidence of adverse events was similar in the two groups.
45|CONCLUSIONS
46|Dapagliflozin reduced the combined risk of worsening heart failure or cardiovas-
47|cular death among patients with heart failure and a mildly reduced or preserved
48|ejection fraction. (Funded by AstraZeneca; DELIVER ClinicalTrials.gov number,
49|NCT03619213.)

5|odium-glucose cotransporter 2
6|(SGLT2) inhibitors, which were originally
7|developed as glucose-lowering agents for
8|the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus, reduce
9|the risk of death and other adverse outcomes
10|among patients with chronic heart failure and
11|a reduced ejection fraction (i.e., a left ventricu-
12|lar ejection fraction of ≤40%) and in those with
13|chronic kidney disease, regardless of the pres-
14|ence or absence of type 2 diabetes mellitus.1-3
15|Current clinical guidelines strongly recommend
16|the use of SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with
17|chronic heart failure and a reduced ejection
18|fraction.4
19|Few pharmacologic treatment options exist
20|for patients with heart failure and a mildly re-
21|duced or preserved left ventricular ejection frac-
22|tion.5,6 Recently, treatment with the SGLT2 in-
23|hibitor empagliflozin was shown to reduce the
24|combined risk of hospitalization for heart fail-
25|ure or cardiovascular death among patients with
26|heart failure and a left ventricular ejection frac-
27|tion of more than 40%, a finding that suggests
28|that the benefits of SGLT2 inhibition may extend
29|to all patients with heart failure, regardless of
30|the left ventricular ejection fraction.7 The bene-
31|fit, which was driven by a reduction in hospital-
32|ization for heart failure, appeared to be attenu-
33|ated in patients with ejection fractions in the
34|highest part (≥65%) of the range.8
35|Several gaps in evidence remain regarding
36|the benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors in patients with
37|heart failure, including whether these benefits
38|are conserved in patients with an ejection frac-
39|tion at the highest end of the ejection fraction
40|spectrum, in patients who start the treatment
41|during or soon after hospitalization, and in pa-
42|tients with a previously reduced ejection fraction
43|that has since improved to more than 40%. We
44|designed the Dapagliflozin Evaluation to Im-
45|prove the Lives of Patients with Preserved Ejec-
46|tion Fraction Heart Failure (DELIVER) trial to
47|test the hypothesis that the SGLT2 inhibitor
48|dapagliflozin would reduce the risk of worsen-
49|ing heart failure or cardiovascular death among
50|patients with a mildly reduced or preserved ejec-
51|tion fraction.
52|Methods
53|Trial Design and Oversight
54|The DELIVER trial was a phase 3, international,
55|multicenter, parallel-group, event-driven, double-
56|blind, randomized, controlled trial in which pa-
57|tients with chronic heart failure and a left ven-
58|tricular ejection fraction of more than 40%
59|received dapagliflozin or matching placebo, in
60|addition to their usual therapy. The steering com-
61|mittee designed and oversaw the conduct of the
62|trial and the analysis of the data in collaboration
63|with the sponsor (AstraZeneca). The trial proto-
64|col was approved by a local or central institu-
65|tional review board at each trial center. The au-
66|thors who had access to the data vouch for the
67|accuracy and completeness of the data, and all
68|the authors vouch for the fidelity of the trial to
69|the protocol. Details regarding the design of the
70|trial are provided in the protocol and in the Sup-
71|plementary Appendix, both of which are avail-
72|able with the full text of this article at NEJM.org.
73|Trial Patients
74|Patients were eligible for enrollment if they were
75|at least 40 years of age; had stabilized heart
76|failure, with or without type 2 diabetes mellitus;
77|had a left ventricular ejection fraction of more
78|than 40%; had evidence of structural heart dis-
79|ease; and had an elevated natriuretic peptide
80|level. Patients who had had a previous left ven-
81|tricular ejection fraction of 40% or less were
82|eligible provided that they had an ejection frac-
83|tion of more than 40% at the time of enroll-
84|ment. Patients could have been enrolled either as
85|outpatients or during hospitalization for heart
86|failure. Detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria
87|have been published previously9 and are provid-
88|ed in Table S1 in the Supplementary Appendix.
89|Trial Procedures and Outcomes
90|All the patients provided written informed con-
91|sent. Those who met the inclusion and exclusion
92|criteria were randomly assigned to receive dapa-
93|gliflozin at a dose of 10 mg once daily or match-
94|ing placebo, in addition to their usual therapy.
95|The primary outcome was a composite of
96|worsening heart failure, which was defined as
97|either an unplanned hospitalization for heart
98|failure or an urgent visit for heart failure, or
99|cardiovascular death. Secondary outcomes were
100|the total number of worsening heart failure
101|events and cardiovascular deaths, the change
102|from baseline in the total symptom score on the
103|Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire
104|(KCCQ; scores range from 0 to 100, with higher
105|scores indicating fewer symptoms and physical
106|limitations) at month 8, cardiovascular death,

14|Statistical Analysis
15|The primary outcome, the occurrence of worsen-
16|ing heart failure or cardiovascular death, was
17|assessed in a time-to-event analysis with the use
18|of a Cox proportional-hazards model, stratified
19|according to diabetes status. This analysis was
20|performed concurrently in the overall population
21|and in patients with a left ventricular ejection
22|fraction of less than 60%, with an alpha level of
23|0.024 used in the former analysis and an alpha
24|level of 0.038 used in the latter analysis (see the
25|Supplementary Methods section and Fig. S1 and
26|Table S2). We estimated that enrollment of 6100
27|patients followed for at least 13.5 months (and
28|up to 39 months) would result in the occurrence
29|of at least 1117 events and would provide the
30|trial with 93% power to detect a hazard ratio of
31|0.80 for the comparison of dapagliflozin and
32|placebo with respect to the primary outcome in
33|the overall population, at a two-sided alpha level
34|of 0.024. All the analyses were performed ac-
35|cording to the intention-to-treat principle. Second-
36|ary analyses were performed with the use of a
37|closed-testing procedure that included a pre-
38|specified hierarchical ordering of the primary
39|and secondary outcomes; these outcomes in-
40|cluded (in hierarchical order) the total number
41|of worsening heart failure events and cardiovas-
42|cular deaths, a decrease in symptom burden as
43|measured by an increase in the KCCQ total
44|symptom score, and cardiovascular death and
45|death from any cause (both of which were as-
46|sessed in a time-to-event analysis). We analyzed
47|the KCCQ total symptom score as a composite
48|outcome based on the rank of the change in
49|score from baseline to month 8, with a corre-
50|sponding win ratio used to estimate the magni-
51|tude of the treatment effect.11-13 We assessed the
52|consistency of the treatment effect on the pri-
53|mary outcome in prespecified subgroups. In
54|separate sensitivity analyses, patient data were
55|censored at the time of coronavirus disease 2019
56|(Covid-19) diagnosis, and death from noncardio-
57|vascular causes was taken into account as a
58|competing risk.14

60|Patients
61|Between August 27, 2018, and December 30,
62|2020, a total of 10,418 patients were screened at
63|353 centers in 20 countries; of these patients,
64|6263 were randomly assigned to receive dapa-
65|gliflozin or matching placebo (Fig. S2). The
66|reasons for exclusion from randomization are
67|provided in Table S3. The demographic and
68|clinical characteristics of the two groups were
69|well balanced at baseline (Table 1 and Table S4).

71|than death in 444 patients (14.2%), and placebo
72|was discontinued for reasons other than death
73|in 442 patients (14.1%). The vital status was
74|known at the end of the trial in all but 2 patients
75|in the dapagliflozin group and 2 patients in the
76|placebo group. The median duration of follow-

23|In this randomized, placebo-controlled trial in-
24|volving patients with heart failure and a mildly
25|reduced or preserved ejection fraction, dapa-
26|gliflozin resulted in a lower risk of the primary
27|composite outcome, worsening heart failure or
28|cardiovascular death, than placebo, with no ap-

30|with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60% or
31|more and those with a left ventricular ejection
32|fraction of less than 60%, or in other subgroups.
33|Each of the three components of this composite
34|outcome was less common in the dapagliflozin
35|group than in the placebo group. In addition,
36|dapagliflozin resulted in fewer total worsening
37|heart failure events and cardiovascular deaths
38|and a lower symptom burden than placebo. The
39|incidence of adverse events was similar to that in
40|the placebo group.
41|In a previous trial (DAPA-HF; Dapagliflozin
42|and Prevention of Adverse Outcomes in Heart
43|Failure), dapagliflozin reduced the risk of wors-
44|ening heart failure or cardiovascular death
45|among patients with heart failure and a left
46|ventricular ejection fraction of 40% or less.1 The
47|results of the DELIVER trial extend those of the
48|DAPA-HF trial to patients with heart failure and
49|a left ventricular ejection fraction of more than
50|40% and are consistent with the overall results
51|of the EMPEROR-Preserved trial (Empagliflozin
52|Outcome Trial in Patients with Chronic Heart
53|Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction), which
54|assessed the effects of empagliflozin in patients
55|with a left ventricular ejection fraction of more
56|than 40%.10 The rationale for the dual primary
57|analyses in our trial (i.e., evaluation of the pri-
58|mary outcome in patients with a left ventricular
59|ejection fraction of less than 60% in addition to
60|the overall patient population) was based on
61|concern about a potential declining benefit in
62|patients with an ejection fraction in the normal
63|range that had been observed in several previous

65|the EMPEROR-Preserved trial suggested some
